# Week 5+ worksheet: time-resolved data
This will serve as an introduction to more complex data and analysis as we increase our skills in R. 

### Importing and clearing data
```{r Lethbridge, warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}
#Immediately, this looks like it is not importing well!
OzoneData <- read_csv("OzoneData.csv")
head(OzoneData)

#Here I've added some line skips, and am re-naming the specific columns to reflect the station names that we have data for
OzoneData <- read_csv("OzoneData.csv", skip = 28, name_repair ="minimal") 

colnames(OzoneData)[1:10] <- paste0(colnames(OzoneData)[1:10], "_O3_Leth")

colnames(OzoneData)[11:20] <-  sub(".1", "", colnames(OzoneData)[11:20])
colnames(OzoneData)[11:20] <- paste0(colnames(OzoneData)[11:20], "_CO_Leth")

colnames(OzoneData)[21:30] <-  sub(".2", "", colnames(OzoneData)[21:30])
colnames(OzoneData)[21:30] <- paste0(colnames(OzoneData)[21:30], "_O3_Calgary")

colnames(OzoneData)[31:40] <-  sub(".3", "", colnames(OzoneData)[31:40])
colnames(OzoneData)[31:40] <- paste0(colnames(OzoneData)[31:40], "_CO_Calgary")

colnames(OzoneData)[41:50] <-  sub(".4", "", colnames(OzoneData)[41:50])
colnames(OzoneData)[41:50] <- paste0(colnames(OzoneData)[41:50], "_O3_Edmonton")

colnames(OzoneData)[51:60] <-  sub(".5", "", colnames(OzoneData)[51:60])
colnames(OzoneData)[51:60] <- paste0(colnames(OzoneData)[51:60], "_CO_Edmonton")

OzoneData <- OzoneData %>%
  select(contains(c("Start", "Measurement", "Flags"))) %>%
  mutate(`Measurement Value_O3_Leth` = `Measurement Value_O3_Leth`*1000)

head(OzoneData)

```

### Plotting data
Let's visualize the hourly ozone mixing ratio for Lethbridge, Edmonton, and Calgary.


```{r plotting, warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}

#Method 1: plotting them all individually
Leth <- ggplot(OzoneData, aes(x = date, y = `Measurement Value_O3_Leth`))+
  geom_point() + 
  theme_bw()+
  ggtitle("Lethbridge")



Leth



#Method 2: plotting them all on the same plot!

#wide form: 
ggplot(OzoneData,
       aes(x= date,
           y = `Measurement Value_O3_Leth`))+
  geom_point(colour = "blue")+
  geom_point(aes(x= date,
                 y = `Measurement Value_O3_Calgary`),
             colour = "red")+
  geom_point(aes(x= date,
                 y = `Measurement Value_O3_Edmonton`),
             colour = "purple")

#Long form



ggplot(OzoneDataLong %>% filter(pollutant == "O3"), aes(x = date , y = measurements, colour = location))+
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw()
             

#Method 3: plotting all three graphs together as one
```

## Diurnal plots 

Let's work to understand how ambient ozone levels depend on the time of day.
```{r diurnal plot,  warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}

#we need to extract hour as a variable from the 'date' column so we can plot it.


#this looks okay! We can start to see the diurnal pattern here. 
ggplot(OzoneLeth, aes(x= Hour, y = measurements))+
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw()

#We can simplify our data by plotting the averages instead of all the data. This reduces the complexity of the data, but theoretically continues to hold all the information (more on that later!)




```

## Openair 
How can packages help us do this quickly?
```{r openair,  warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}

library(openair)

#It can easily select different part of your data by time

FebData <- selectByDate(OzoneDataLong, month = "Feb")
head(FebData)

#It can quickly plot the data as a function of all time variables

timeVariation(
  OzoneDataLong %>%
    filter(location == "Leth", pollutant == "O3"),
  pollutant = "measurements",
  ylab = "O3 (ppb)"
)

timePlot(OzoneDataLong %>% filter(pollutant == "O3"), 
  pollutant = "measurements",
  type = "location",
  avg.time = "month")

diurnal <- timeVariation(
    OzoneDataLong %>% 
      filter(location == "Leth",
             pollutant == "O3"),
     pollutant = "measurements",
     x = "hour")

plot(diurnal, subset="hour")

```
